analysis.one_liner: Caps overdraft fees at one per month and bans fees on declined debit transactions.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap bank overdraft fees never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 116th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: Banks make tens of billions of dollars a year charging fees when a customer's account briefly goes negative, often on small debit card purchases. This bill would cap those fees at one per month and six per year, require them to be proportional to the overdraft, ban fees when a debit hold caused the overdraft, ban nonsufficient-funds fees on ATM and debit card transactions, and require clear disclosures so customers can decline overdraft 'protection' without being penalized. The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau would write the rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Checking account customers who occasionally overdraw—disproportionately low- and moderate-income households—would keep money they now lose to fees, and would see fees capped, priced transparently, and avoidable.

how_it_helps.text: Caps overdraft coverage fees at no more than one per calendar month and six per calendar year per account [S2][S3].
Requires fees to be reasonable and proportional to the overdraft amount, and bans fees when the overdraft results only from a debit hold larger than the actual transaction [S2][S3].
Prohibits nonsufficient fund fees on ATM and debit card transactions, so a customer who declines overdraft coverage is not charged for a declined purchase [S2][S3].

Requires clear marketing disclosures that a transaction may simply be declined with no fee if the customer does not opt in, prompt notification when coverage is used, and posting of transactions in an order that minimizes fees [S2][S3].
Prohibits reporting negative information to consumer reporting agencies when overdrafts and fees are repaid under a coverage program [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and credit unions would lose overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fee revenue, a multi-billion-dollar income stream that comes mainly from frequent overdrafters with low balances.

drawbacks.text: Banks argue that if they cannot charge fees for covering overdrafts, they may decline to cover them at all, leaving customers with bounced transactions instead of paid ones [S3 — the bill acknowledges institutions may retain discretion to reject overdrafts].
Fee revenue funds 'free' checking for other customers; capping overdraft fees could push banks to raise other account fees or minimum balance requirements, shifting costs to different customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits—fees capped, priced proportionally, and clearly disclosed for customers who can least afford them—outweigh the cost to banks, though some customers who currently rely on overdraft coverage might see fewer transactions paid. The bill lets institutions still cover overdrafts without fees, softening that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Introduced by Rep. Carolyn Maloney on September 9, 2019, with 19 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S4].
Referred to the House Committee on Financial Services on September 9, 2019; no further action was taken [S5].
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote occurred before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and credit unions keep collecting overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fee revenue that the bill would have capped and limited. Consumers who overdraw their accounts continue paying the current fee structure.

for.name: Rep. Carolyn B. Maloney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 19 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after referral.

sides.party_line_note: All listed sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored, and the committee took no action [S4][S5].

industries.note: Overdraft and nonsufficient-funds fees are a major, highly profitable revenue stream drawn disproportionately from customers with low balances; the bill caps, limits, and discloses them.
